task: MYP Personal Project report: describe your goal, global context, process, product and reflection.
text:
Personal Project Report: A Low-Cost Hydroponic Herb Unit for the School Canteen

Goal and global context

My goal was to design, build and test a low-cost vertical hydroponic unit, made mostly from reused materials, that could grow basil, mint and coriander for our school canteen. The global context is globalization and sustainability. The reason I chose it is that our canteen imports most of its fresh herbs. When I asked the canteen manager, Mrs Okafor, she said that herbs arrive in plastic clamshell packs and about a third go off before they are used. I wanted to know if a small system could replace some of that supply in a way that is cheap enough for a school to copy.

My personal interest comes from my grandfather's farm, where water shortages every summer made me aware of how wasteful ordinary irrigation can be. I had never built anything electrical or plumbed anything, so the project was also a real stretch for me.

Research and what it changed in my plan

I started with three kinds of source. First, I read the FAO report on urban agriculture and a university extension guide on nutrient film and deep water culture, which explained that hydroponics can use up to 90 percent less water than soil, but need electricity for pumps (FAO, 2020). Second, I interviewed Mrs Okafor and a science technician, Mr Bell. Third, I looked at three commercial kits online. The kits cost between 90 and 240 dollars, which is far above what a school club could afford, and this became my main design problem.

The research changed my plan in two ways. I had planned to use a nutrient film system, but Mr Bell warned me that thin channels clog and the plants die within a day if a pump fails. I switched to a simple ebb and flow design with a reservoir, which is more forgiving. I also learned that my first idea of growing six plant types was unrealistic, so I narrowed it to three herbs with similar nutrient needs. I recorded both changes in my process journal on the day they happened, because I wanted my decisions to be traceable.

Success criteria

I wrote my success criteria after the research so they would be realistic. I made them measurable, and I included one for the global context.

1. The unit costs less than 60 dollars to build, counting reused items at a fair second-hand price.
2. The unit uses no more than 8 litres of water a week, measured by topping up the reservoir.
3. At least 8 of 12 seedlings survive for four weeks, and basil grows at least 15 cm in that time, measured with a ruler weekly.
4. Mrs Okafor harvests enough herbs for at least two canteen recipes during the project period.
5. A one-page build guide is written clearly enough that a student who was not involved can follow it, tested with two classmates.
6. The soil-free system uses less water per plant than the same herbs in soil pots, compared against a control group of 6 pots.

Planning

I had ten weeks, so I worked backwards from the date I needed to submit this report. I divided the project into research (weeks 1 to 2), design and buying parts (weeks 3 to 4), build and test the pump (week 5), planting and monitoring (weeks 6 to 9), and writing up (week 10). I built in a buffer because I knew from my last design project that things take longer than expected. I used a Gantt chart in a spreadsheet and checked it every Sunday. Where I was behind, I recorded why. For example, the pump arrived a week late, so I used the waiting time to prepare the seedling trays and write the build guide draft.

Applying skills

Thinking skills. The hardest design problem was making a timer-controlled flood cycle without buying an expensive controller. I generated three options: a cheap mechanical timer, a microcontroller, or a float switch. I compared them on cost, reliability and how easy they would be for another student to repeat. The microcontroller was the cheapest but it needed code, and I decided against it because criterion 5 asks for a guide a beginner can follow. I chose a 6 dollar mechanical plug timer set to flood for 15 minutes four times a day. My first test failed because the overflow pipe was too high, and the tray did not drain. I corrected this by cutting the standpipe by 2 cm, and I measured the drain time (it went from 40 minutes to 9).

Research skills. I kept a source list and I judged them. The FAO report is credible but written about large-scale farming, so I treated its water figure as an upper bound. A YouTube video claimed basil grows 30 cm in two weeks, and I ignored it because it had no data and sold a product. My own data showed average growth of 17 cm in four weeks, which is much closer to the extension guide.

Self-management skills. I kept a log of hours (about 62 in total) and I noticed in week 3 that I was spending too long on the design drawing. I set a rule of one hour a day for drawing, and I finished on time. I also negotiated with the school to use the back of the science block, and I wrote a short email to the head of facilities asking permission, explaining the water and electrical safety measures, which included a residual current device.

Communication and social skills. I made a short presentation to the Eco Club in week 4 and received feedback that my diagram did not show where the water flows. I redrew it with arrows. When Mrs Okafor was not available, I corresponded by email and kept the questions specific, for example asking which herbs she used most.

Evaluation of the product against my success criteria

Criterion 1 was met: the total cost was 54.80 dollars. The pump (14 dollars) and timer (6 dollars) were the main cost, and I reused a plastic storage crate, PVC offcuts and mesh pots from the recycling store. Criterion 2 was met: average weekly top-up was 5.6 litres, though in the hottest week it reached 7.9, just under my limit. Criterion 3 was partly met: 10 of 12 seedlings survived and basil grew a mean of 17 cm, but two coriander plants bolted early in the heat, which means coriander is probably not suitable for a sunny outdoor spot. Criterion 4 was met only narrowly: the first harvest of 120 g of basil and 80 g of mint was used in a pesto pasta and a mint raita, but a second recipe needed more than I had grown. Criterion 5 was met after changes: my first guide had 14 steps and both testers got stuck on step 6, where I had not named the pipe fitting. After I added a photo and a parts list, both testers finished in about 40 minutes. Criterion 6 was met with a caveat: the hydroponic plants used about 0.47 litres per plant per week against 0.9 for soil, which is 48 percent lower, but my control group was small and the soil pots were in a shadier place, so the comparison is not fully fair.

Overall, the product achieved five of six criteria fully or mostly, and the weakest area was output volume. The unit works, but it is too small to supply a canteen. A realistic judgement is that it is a good demonstration and teaching tool, and that scaling it would need at least four units.

Reflection on my learning

I learned that testing early is better than planning for a perfect design. My overflow problem would have ruined the whole project if I had found it in week 7. I also learned that I am better at technical problem solving than at asking for help. In week 5 I struggled for two days with a leaking fitting before asking Mr Bell, who solved it in five minutes with plumber's tape. After that I set a rule of asking after one hour of being stuck.

If I did the project again I would grow in two smaller units to protect against a single failure, choose a shadier site, and keep better temperature records, because I only have the weather station data and not data from the unit itself. I would also test with more seedlings so that the soil comparison is statistically stronger.

Impact on me and on others

For me, the project changed how I think about food. I now look at the water footprint of what I eat, and I have decided to take Design and Environmental Systems at DP. For the school, the Eco Club has asked me to run a workshop to build two more units next term, and Mrs Okafor said she would pay for the herbs seeds. A limitation is that the impact on global sustainability is small, because one unit saves only a few litres. Its larger value is educational: 14 students visited it during the open day and several asked for the build guide. I measured the guide's usefulness by whether strangers could follow it, and that is the part I am proudest of.

Bibliography

Food and Agriculture Organization of the United Nations (2020) Urban and peri-urban agriculture: a guide for city planners. Rome: FAO.
Resh, H. (2013) Hydroponic Food Production. 7th edn. Boca Raton: CRC Press.
Interview with Mrs Okafor, canteen manager, 12 February.
Interview with Mr Bell, science technician, 15 February.

task: MYP Personal Project report: describe your goal, global context, process, product and reflection.
text:
Personal Project: Writing and Recording a Four-Song EP

Goal and global context

My goal was to write, arrange and record a four-song EP of original music with a guitar and a free recording program. My global context is personal and cultural expression, because I wanted to see how my background as a Nigerian-British teenager could be reflected in the lyrics and the music. I chose this because I have played guitar for five years but I have only ever played other people's songs, and I wanted to challenge myself to be a creator for once.

Research

I began by listening to artists that mix different cultural influences, such as Burna Boy, Ed Sheeran and Tems, and I took notes on how they use rhythm, language and instruments. I read two articles about the afrobeats genre and its history, and I watched a tutorial series on songwriting by a professional producer. I also interviewed my music teacher, Mr Daniels, who told me that a good EP should have a consistent sound, and that the order of the songs matters. I learned that afrobeats usually has a syncopated rhythm at about 100 to 110 beats per minute, so I decided to keep my songs between 95 and 115 BPM.

I also tried to find out what free recording programs I could use. I compared GarageBand, Audacity and BandLab, and I picked BandLab because it works on a school laptop and lets me record several tracks.

Success criteria

My success criteria were:
1. The EP will have four original songs, each between 2.5 and 4 minutes long.
2. At least two songs will include lyrics in both English and Yoruba, to show my cultural background.
3. The recordings will have a clean sound, without distortion or background noise, judged by Mr Daniels and two friends using a scorecard out of 10.
4. I will finish and upload the EP to a streaming platform before the end of the project.
5. I will receive an average score of at least 7 out of 10 from ten listeners in a survey.

Plan

I set myself a timetable of ten weeks. In weeks 1 to 2 I did research, in weeks 3 to 6 I wrote one song every week and a half, in weeks 7 to 9 I recorded and mixed, and in week 10 I uploaded and wrote the report. I made a weekly checklist in my notebook. I did not manage to keep to this plan exactly. Song 3 took me almost three weeks because I was not happy with the chorus, so I shortened the recording time. I decided to record the drums using a free drum loop instead of recording a real drum kit, which I had initially wanted to do, because I could not get access to the music room in time.

Applying skills

Creative thinking: I used a method where I wrote the chord progression first, then hummed melodies over it, and only wrote the lyrics at the end. This helped me because my lyrics used to be forced. For my song Home Is Two Places I used a Yoruba phrase that my grandmother says, and I asked her to check my spelling and meaning. For the second song I tried to write about leaving a friend behind when I changed school.

Technical skills: I had to learn to use a digital audio workstation. In the beginning my recordings had too much hiss from the laptop microphone. I watched a video about gain staging and then moved my recording to a wardrobe with coats in it, which deadened the echo. The result was much cleaner. I also learned to use EQ and a little reverb, although my final mixes are still quite basic.

Self-management: I used a checklist and I kept a recording diary. I did fall behind in weeks 5 and 6 because of exams, and I handled this by working at weekends. I contacted Mr Daniels for feedback every two weeks, and I used the feedback to change the bridge in Song 1, which he said was too long.

More about how the songs were written

Song 1, Home Is Two Places, was the first one I finished. The idea came from the way I switch between two ways of talking depending on whether I am at home or at school. I wrote the chorus first, using four chords, and the verses came afterwards. I recorded the guitar three times because the first two takes were out of time. I think the metronome click helped, though at first it made me tense and my playing sounded stiff, so I turned it down a little.

Song 2, Left Behind, was slower, about 95 BPM, and I used a fingerpicking pattern. This was the most personal song and it was the one I found hardest to sing, because I do not have a strong voice. I recorded the vocal at night when the house was quiet, and I did about eight takes. In the end I used pieces from different takes, which is called comping, and I learned about it from a tutorial. Mr Daniels said the second verse was the best vocal on the EP.

Song 3, Lagos Rain, took longest. I wanted it to sound like afrobeats, so I used a drum loop and a bass line that I played on guitar an octave lower. The problem was that the chorus did not feel different from the verse. Mr Daniels suggested that I raise the melody by a few notes and add a second guitar part, and this made the chorus feel bigger. Song 4, Quiet Hours, was a short instrumental with a little humming, which I wrote in two days when I was running out of time.

Product

I finished four songs: Home Is Two Places (3:20), Left Behind (2:50), Lagos Rain (3:35) and Quiet Hours (2:40). The EP is called Two Places. I uploaded it to SoundCloud on week 10 (I had planned to use Spotify, but distributing there needs a paid service).

Evaluation against the success criteria

Criterion 1 was met, since all four songs are between 2:40 and 3:35. Criterion 2 was met for two songs (Home Is Two Places and Lagos Rain), which include Yoruba lines in the chorus. Criterion 3 was partly met. Mr Daniels gave a 7 out of 10 for sound and said that the vocals were slightly too quiet compared with the guitar, and my two friends gave 8 and 6. The average is 7, which is acceptable but not as clean as I wanted. Criterion 4 was partly met because I uploaded to SoundCloud and not a major streaming service. For criterion 5, I got ten responses and the average score was 7.4, so it was met, although most of the listeners were my friends and family, which may make the score higher than it would be with strangers.

Reflection

I have learned a lot about myself and the process. I found out that I like writing music more than I thought, and that the part I find hardest is finishing. I often started a new idea before the last one was done. I think that I have improved in my self-management because I managed to complete all four songs even with exams. I also learned that feedback can be hard to hear, as when Mr Daniels said that my bridge was boring, but that it improved the song.

A problem I did not solve was the balance between the vocals and the guitar. Both Mr Daniels and one listener mentioned it, and I could hear it myself when I listened on headphones, but I did not know enough about mixing to fix it. I tried turning the guitar down, but then it sounded thin. This suggests that I need to learn more about compression, and next time I would watch a tutorial on this earlier in the project rather than in the last week.

There are things I would do differently. I would have recorded a real drum kit, and I would have asked someone with experience to mix the tracks. I would also have gathered feedback from people I did not know. My product is good for a first attempt, but the sound is not professional.

The project has had an impact on me because I now feel more confident calling myself a songwriter. It also had an impact on my family: my grandmother cried when she listened to the Yoruba lines, which showed me that the music meant something to her as well. Next I want to perform the songs live at the school's talent show.

Sources

Burna Boy (2019) African Giant. Atlantic Records.
Oyelaran, T. (2019) A short history of afrobeats. Music Magazine website.
Interview with Mr Daniels, music teacher.
BandLab help centre tutorials.

text:
Personal Project Report: Making a Short Film About Bullying

Introduction

For my personal project I decided to make a short film about bullying in schools. My goal is to make a film that is good and that will make people understand more about bullying. The global context I chose is fairness and development, because bullying is not fair and it happens all over the world. I chose this topic because I have seen bullying at my school and I think it is a big problem that is not talked about enough. I also like film and I want to study media at university.

I thought that making a film would be a good way to show people about this issue because film can be very powerful and a lot of people watch videos on their phones.

Success criteria

My success criteria are:
1. The film will be good quality.
2. The film will show bullying in a realistic way.
3. People will like the film and understand the message.
4. I will finish the film on time.
5. I will learn lots of new skills.

Research

First I did research about bullying. I went on Google and found some websites about bullying, including Wikipedia, which said that bullying is repeated aggressive behaviour where there is a power imbalance. I also read an article from a charity website that said one in three students experience bullying. I learned that there are different kinds of bullying such as physical, verbal and cyberbullying. I then watched some short films about bullying on YouTube so I could get ideas. I liked one called Validation but it was about something else. After that I wrote down some ideas in my notebook.

Why I chose this topic

I have thought about this topic for a long time. When I was in Year 8 there was a boy in my class who was always picked on and nobody did anything. I felt bad about it. I do not want to say his name, but this was the reason I wanted to do something about bullying. I think many people at my school do not understand how it feels, and I thought that if I made a film they might see it in a different way. I also think that films can change how people think. For example, there are lots of famous films that made people think differently about things, so I thought I could do the same on a smaller scale.

I talked to my parents about it first. My dad said that I should be careful about the topic because it can make people upset. My mum said it was a very good idea. I also talked to my form tutor and she said she would help if I needed anything. I felt supported, and this made me want to do the project more.

Process journal

Week 1: I chose my topic and wrote my proposal. I told my supervisor, Ms Rahman, and she said it was a good idea.

Week 2: I did my research and started to write the script. I decided that the film would be about a boy called Sam who is bullied by a group of classmates and in the end a friend helps him.

Week 3: I finished the first script. It was 4 pages long. I showed it to my friend Hamza and he said it was okay but the ending was too happy.

Week 4: I changed the ending so that it is more open. I also started to look for actors. I asked three of my friends and they said yes. I made a list of locations: the school corridor, the playground and a bedroom.

Week 5: We filmed the first scenes in the corridor after school. It took longer than I expected because the actors kept laughing. I used my phone to film and a tripod that I borrowed from my cousin.

Week 6: We filmed the playground scene. It rained so we had to stop and I did not get everything I wanted. I had to rewrite one scene so that it would happen in a classroom instead.

Week 7: I did the classroom scene and the bedroom scene. I was very tired this week because of tests.

Week 8: I started editing on a free app called CapCut. It was hard at first but I watched some tutorials. I added music from a copyright-free website.

Week 9: I finished editing and I showed the film to some people. They said they liked it. I fixed the sound in one scene because it was too quiet.

Week 10: I wrote the report and I prepared the exhibition.

Extra notes on weeks 5 to 9

On the day of filming in the corridor I arrived early to set up the tripod. I had made a shot list with 14 shots, but we only got 9 of them that day. I felt stressed because the caretaker said we had to leave at 4.30. Hamza, who played one of the bullies, was very good at being serious, but the other boy, Ali, kept laughing every time he had to say his line, so we did about 12 takes. At the end of the day I was tired but happy. I thanked everyone and I promised I would give them credit in the film.

In week 6 I was disappointed about the rain. I had planned the playground scene for a long time and I felt that all my work was wasted. I spoke to Ms Rahman and she said that filmmakers have to be flexible. I thought about it that evening and I decided to move the scene indoors. This made me feel better. The classroom scene was good in the end because the light from the window made it look more serious.

In week 8 I was very nervous about editing because I had never done it before. I watched about six videos on YouTube. At first, I put all the clips in the wrong order and the story was confusing, but I fixed it. I spent nearly the whole weekend on it. I cut the film from nine minutes to six minutes and twenty seconds, because my friend said that it was too long and slow. I cannot say how many hours I spent because I did not write them down, but I think it was a lot.

In week 9 I showed the film to my mum, my brother and two friends. My mum cried a little and my brother said it was cool. One friend said the music was too loud, so I lowered it.

Applying skills

During the project I used lots of ATL skills. I used communication skills when I talked to my actors and my supervisor. I used organization skills because I made a plan and I kept to the deadlines most of the time. I used thinking skills when I was coming up with the idea and the script. I used research skills when I searched for information about bullying, and I used social skills when I was working with my friends, who were the actors. I also used creative thinking skills for the story, and reflection skills at the end of each week when I wrote in my journal. I found that these skills were really important for completing the project.

The product

The final film is 6 minutes and 20 seconds long. It is called Not Alone. It shows Sam being pushed in the corridor, called names in the playground, and then receiving cruel messages on his phone in his bedroom. At the end, a classmate, Priya, sits with him at lunch. It has background music and some subtitles. I think the film is realistic and it sends a clear message.

More about my feelings and my skills

During the project I felt many different things. In the beginning I felt excited, in the middle I felt stressed, and at the end I felt proud. I think my communication skills have improved a lot because I had to give instructions to my actors. At the start I was shy, and by the end I could tell people what to do. I also think my organization skills improved even though I did not always keep to the plan. I think that I have become more mature as a person because of this project, and I learned to be responsible for my own work.

I believe the global context was important because bullying affects many people around the world. According to the charity article, it happens in almost every country. My film was made in my school but it could be about any school in the world. I think the message of being kind is a universal one.

Evaluation

I think my project was successful overall. The film is good quality because I used a tripod and I edited it carefully. It shows bullying in a realistic way because it includes many different types and the actors were convincing. When I showed the film to people at the exhibition, they said they liked it and understood the message. I finished the film on time, although I had to stay up late in week 9. I learned lots of new skills such as editing, directing, and managing a team.

Some problems were that the weather caused delays and the sound was not perfect in some scenes because I only used my phone microphone. Some of my actors were not very serious. If I had more time I would use a better camera and microphone.

Reflection

This project taught me many things. I learned that making a film is a lot of work and takes much longer than I expected. I also learned that you need to be patient when working with other people. I am happy with the film and I think it will help people to think about bullying. I now know that I want to continue studying film and I think the project helped me prepare for my future. The project also made me think about how important it is to be kind.

If I did it again I would plan more carefully and I would test the sound before filming. I think I did a good job in my project and I am proud of what I achieved.

Bibliography

Wikipedia. Bullying.
Charity website article on bullying statistics.
Validation (short film) on YouTube.
CapCut tutorial videos on YouTube.

text:
My Personal Project

My project is about baking. My goal is to bake a cake. I chose baking because I like to eat cakes and my mum bakes a lot at home so I wanted to learn how to do it as well. The global context is personal and cultural expression because baking is part of culture.

What I did

First I looked on the internet for recipes. I found a lot of recipes for chocolate cake, vanilla cake and red velvet cake. I decided to make a chocolate cake with white icing because it is my favourite. I wrote the ingredients in a list: flour, sugar, eggs, butter, cocoa powder and milk. I went with my mum to the shop to buy them.

Then I made the cake on a Saturday. My mum helped me with the oven because it is hot. I mixed the butter and sugar first and then I added the eggs and then the flour. I put it in the tin and baked it for 35 minutes. The first cake was not very good because it was a bit flat and dry. I think I left it in too long.

The next weekend I made the cake again and it was better. I put icing on it and I decorated it with some strawberries. I took photos of it and I showed it to my family. They all said it was delicious.

Success criteria

My success criteria were:
- The cake should taste nice.
- The cake should look good.
- I should learn how to bake.

Problems

I had some problems with this project. The first cake was flat so I was a bit sad about it. My mum said that it happens to everyone. The icing was also quite hard to put on because it was too runny the first time, and it dripped off the cake. I added more sugar and it got better. Also the oven at home is quite old so it is difficult to know what temperature it is, but my mum knows how to use it. I did not take lots of photos of the first cake because I did not like it.

Skills

I used time management because I had to make the cake before the deadline. I used communication skills because I talked to my mum and my teacher. I also used research skills because I looked on the internet.

Evaluation

I think my project went well. The cake tasted nice and it looked good, so I met my success criteria. I learned how to bake a cake, which is useful. My family liked it. Some things went wrong, for example the first cake was flat, but the second one was better.

Reflection

I learned a lot from this project. I learned that baking takes time and you need to follow the recipe. I think I improved at baking and in the future I will bake more cakes. I would like to try making a bigger cake for my brother's birthday. I enjoyed the project and I am glad I chose it.

Personal Project Report: Building a Website for the School Recycling Club

Introduction and goal

My goal for my personal project was to design and build a website for our school recycling club, so that students could find out about recycling and sign up for the club. The global context I selected is globalization and sustainability. I picked this because the recycling club does not have a way of telling people what it does, and I like computing. I have never built a full website before, so I knew it would be a challenge for me.

My success criteria are that the website works, that it looks good, that it has information about recycling, and that students use it. I also wanted to learn how to code in HTML and CSS.

Week 1

In the first week I met my supervisor, Mr Chen, and we talked about my idea. He told me to make a plan. I made a plan on a piece of paper with the weeks written down and what I would do in each week. I also made a folder on my computer for all my files. I used my organization skills to do this. I wrote my first journal entry and I felt excited about the project.

Week 2

In week 2 I did research. I looked at some other school websites and some websites about recycling. I wrote down the things I liked, such as the colours and the menus. I also looked at a tutorial about HTML. I started to learn the tags, such as heading and paragraph. It was quite hard at the beginning, but after two days it became easier. I used research skills and self-management skills this week because I had to find the information by myself and I had to manage my time. I wrote in my journal that I should practise more.

In the middle of week 2 I also had to decide what programs to use. I asked my cousin, who is at university, and he said I should use Visual Studio Code, so I downloaded it. It took a while to install because the school wifi was slow and I had to do it at home. I opened it and wrote my first line of code and the page said hello world, which made me happy. On Thursday I stayed behind after school with Mr Chen to ask him some questions about folders and file names. I used communication skills and self-management skills.

Week 3

In week 3 I drew the design of the website. I drew five pages: the home page, an about page, a how to recycle page, a news page and a sign-up page. I used coloured pencils and chose green and blue for the colours. I showed my drawing to my friend Aisha and she said it looked nice. I used communication skills when I asked for her opinion. I also looked for photos online to use on the website, and I found some on a free website.

At the end of week 3 I also wrote a list of what the recycling club does, which I got by talking to Ms Patel, the teacher in charge. She said that the club meets on Wednesdays, collects paper from classrooms, and organises a collection of old phones each term. I put this in my notebook so that I could use it on the about page. I also decided on a name for the site, which was Green Team. I thought about other names for a while, like Recycle Hub and Eco Squad, but my friends liked Green Team the most. I used thinking skills and social skills for this.

Week 4

In week 4 I started to code the home page. I wrote the HTML for the heading, the menu and the pictures. Then I made it look better by adding CSS. I had a problem because the menu was in the wrong place, and I spent two hours trying to fix it. In the end I looked it up on a forum and found the answer, which was to use something called flexbox. I used thinking skills to solve the problem. I felt happy when it worked.

On Monday of week 4 I made a new file for the CSS, and I linked it to the HTML file. I was confused about why my colours were not changing and it turned out that I had spelled the file name wrong. I felt silly but I fixed it. On Wednesday I added a picture of a recycling bin and a banner. The banner was too big so I made it smaller. On Friday I looked at the whole home page and I was quite pleased with it, but the text was hard to read because the green was too light. I changed the colour. I used technology skills and thinking skills this week.

Week 5

In week 5 I made the about page and the how to recycle page. I wrote the text for them using information from the internet, such as which items can be recycled and which cannot. I made a table to show the different colours of bins. I put the pages online using a free hosting site. I used technology skills this week.

In week 5, on Tuesday, I wrote the about page and I included the information about the club meeting times. On Thursday I wrote the how to recycle page. It took a long time to type because I wanted to be correct, so I looked at three different websites to check which things go in which bin. Then on the weekend I learned how to upload the site to a free hosting service, which was complicated because I had to make an account and verify my email. I made a note of my password in my notebook. When the site was online I sent the link to my mum and she opened it on her phone. I used research skills, self-management skills and communication skills.

Week 6

In week 6 I was ill for two days so I did not do as much as I wanted. I made the news page but it only has one article. I used self-management skills when I returned to work and tried to catch up. I wrote in my journal that I need to manage my time better.

When I came back to school after being ill, my friends told me what I missed in other lessons, so I spent the first two days catching up on homework as well as on my project. task: Does the use of models increase our understanding of the world more than it distorts it? Discuss with reference to two areas of knowledge.
text:
Every model is a deliberate falsification. A map that included every pebble would be as large as the territory and as useless, so its makers leave things out, and those omissions are what make it work. The statistician George Box put the point in a famous line: all models are wrong, but some are useful. The title asks me to weigh understanding against distortion, which assumes that they pull in opposite directions. I will argue that they are often the same act viewed from two sides, and that the better question is whether a model's distortions are of a kind its users know about and can correct. By a model I mean a simplified representation of a system, built to explain or predict it. I will examine this in the natural sciences and the human sciences, using the London Underground map, epidemiological modelling during the covid-19 pandemic, and the rational actor model in economics.

The most direct case for models increasing understanding is that simplification reveals structure that complexity hides. Harry Beck's 1931 map of the London Underground is the clearest example. Beck abandoned geographical accuracy, straightened the lines into vertical, horizontal and 45 degree angles, and spaced the stations almost evenly. What passengers needed to know was the order of stations and where to change, and the map delivers exactly that. It is a model in the sense of the definition above, because it represents a system by deliberately discarding information. The knowledge question this raises is: can a representation be better at conveying knowledge precisely because it is less accurate? I think the answer is yes, but only relative to a purpose. The Tube map is excellent for navigating the network and poor for walking, as many tourists discover when they take a train between two stations that are a few hundred metres apart. So the same distortion that creates understanding for one purpose creates a false belief for another. This suggests that the title's comparison is incomplete without asking what the understanding is for.

The natural sciences give a stronger version of the claim, because here models are expected to predict and not merely to organise. Consider the epidemiological models used in March 2020. The Imperial College report by Ferguson and colleagues estimated that without any intervention Britain might see around 500,000 deaths, and this contributed to the government's decision to impose a lockdown. The model divided the population into compartments (susceptible, infected, recovered) and assumed certain contact patterns and a reproduction number. Its distortions were substantial. Contact patterns were treated as averages, people were assumed not to change their behaviour spontaneously, and the key parameters were estimated from early and poor data. Critics were right that the output looked precise while the inputs were uncertain. Yet the model also increased understanding in a way that no other method could have done in the time available: it made visible the exponential nature of spread, and it showed that the time to act was days and not months. A model can therefore be wrong about the number and right about the shape of the problem. I would argue that the knowledge claim it supported was not "500,000 people will die" but "unmitigated spread would overwhelm hospitals", and that claim was much more robust than the figure.

That distinction brings me to a limit of my argument. It might be objected that I am too generous, since the figure was widely reported and policy was shaped by its apparent precision. If a model's distortions are invisible to the people who rely on it, the model is dangerous however well it organises the data. Here the perspective of the modeller and the perspective of the user differ. A modeller such as Ferguson knows the confidence intervals, whereas a journalist or a politician receives one headline number. The knowledge produced is only as good as the way it is communicated. I think this is a real weakness in the natural sciences, whose authority comes from a method that is self-critical, but whose public use of models is often not. So I would qualify my claim: models increase understanding for those who know what was left out, and may distort for those who do not. The difference lies in the community of knowers, not in the model.

Does this change when we move from natural to human sciences? In economics, the standard model of the rational actor, sometimes called homo economicus, assumes that individuals have stable preferences and maximise their own utility. This model is the foundation of supply and demand analysis and it has allowed economists to predict, for example, that a rise in the price of cigarettes through tax will lower smoking. The knowledge it produces is real. But it is also a stronger distortion than that of the Tube map, because the system it represents, human beings, can respond to being modelled. The behavioural economists Kahneman and Tversky showed through experiments that people systematically violate the assumptions: they weigh losses more heavily than equal gains, and they are affected by how a choice is framed. A rational actor would not do either of these. A defender of the model would reply, rightly I think, that it was never meant to describe individuals, only to predict aggregate behaviour, and that in many markets the errors cancel out. The 2008 financial crisis, however, is a case where they did not cancel out. Models that assumed independent, rational investors underestimated the way that panic spreads, and many institutions held risks which their models told them were negligible.

What is significant here is that the model also shaped the world it described. If traders and regulators believe that markets are efficient, they act in ways that make them less careful, so the model is not only a representation but also a cause. The sociologist Donald MacKenzie has called this the performativity of economic models. This is a feature of the human sciences that the natural sciences largely lack, since planets do not read astronomy. It suggests a second knowledge question: when a model changes the behaviour of what it models, does it make sense to ask whether it is accurate at all? I think it does, but accuracy has to be judged at two moments, before and after the model is adopted. This makes the human sciences more exposed to the distortion side of the title, and it explains why economists have turned to more varied models rather than one dominant one.

A different perspective is the instrumentalist view in the philosophy of science, held by thinkers who believe that models should be judged by their usefulness and not by their truth. On this view the question of distortion hardly arises, since a model never claimed to be true. I find this too easy. If the Tube map were only to be judged by use, the tourist walking in the wrong direction would have no complaint. We do care about whether a model is true to the world in the respects that matter, and the realist position captures this better. But the instrumentalist is right that no model is true in every respect, and that demanding so would leave us with no models at all.

Taking the examples together, a pattern appears. The Tube map's distortions were fixed and known, and almost no one was misled. The epidemiological model's distortions were large but disclosed in the report, and were misleading mainly in the way they were reported. The rational actor model's distortions were partly hidden, partly inherent to the subject, and partly created by the model itself. As we move from the first to the third, the balance shifts. So my answer to the title is qualified. Models increase our understanding more than they distort it where the system is stable, where the uncertainties are documented and where the people using the model know what it left out. They distort more where the system responds to the model, where precision is mistaken for accuracy, and where one model is allowed to become the only way of seeing.

This changes how I think about my own knowledge. Much of what I believe about the world, about climate, markets or health, comes to me through models that I never see, summarised in a single number or a chart. The right response is not to distrust models, since the alternative would be to understand nothing about systems too large to observe directly, but to ask the question that Box implies: wrong in what way, and for whom?

task: To what extent does the passage of time change what counts as knowledge?
text:
We often assume that knowledge is permanent, but a look at history suggests otherwise. Beliefs which were once held with great confidence have been replaced, sometimes within a single lifetime. This essay will consider to what extent the passage of time changes what counts as knowledge, looking at the natural sciences and at history. I will argue that time changes what we accept as knowledge but does not always change what is true, and that the real difficulty is that we cannot easily tell the difference from inside our own period. The main knowledge question is: if what we call knowledge can be overturned, was it ever really knowledge?

In this essay, knowledge means justified belief that is accepted by a community of knowers on good evidence. This definition already suggests that time matters, because evidence and justification change. A belief that was well justified in 1700 could be unjustified now.

A good example from the natural sciences is Newton's theory of gravity. For more than two hundred years it counted as knowledge. It predicted the motion of the planets with astonishing accuracy and it was used to discover Neptune in 1846 from irregularities in the orbit of Uranus. Then in 1915 Einstein's general relativity explained the orbit of Mercury, which Newtonian physics could not, and observations during the 1919 solar eclipse supported Einstein. Newton's theory was displaced. However, it was not simply thrown away. Engineers still use Newtonian mechanics to design bridges and to send spacecraft to the Moon, because at everyday speeds and masses the difference is too small to matter. This shows that the passage of time does not always cancel earlier knowledge. Instead it can limit it, showing where it applies. So in the natural sciences, time changes the status of knowledge claims from universal to approximate. A critic might say that if Newton's theory was only approximately right then it was never knowledge. But I think this sets the standard too high. If knowledge had to be final, almost nothing in science would count.

The history of medicine gives an example that is less comfortable. For centuries doctors believed in miasma theory, which says that disease was caused by bad air. This was not a foolish belief, since it fitted with the fact that diseases were common near swamps and in dirty areas. In the 1840s Ignaz Semmelweis noticed that women who gave birth in a ward attended by doctors died of childbed fever more often than women attended by midwives, and he suggested that doctors carried something from the autopsy room on their hands. When he made them wash their hands with chlorinated lime, deaths fell sharply. But he could not explain why, and the medical community mostly rejected his idea. Only after Pasteur and Koch developed germ theory did it become accepted. This is an example where the passage of time changed what counted as knowledge, but the earlier rejection was not only caused by lack of evidence. Semmelweis had evidence but he did not have a theory that fit what doctors already believed, and he was also rude to his critics. So what counts as knowledge is not decided by evidence alone but by what the community is prepared to accept, which changes with time.

This links to the role of perspectives. People in the nineteenth century looked at the evidence through the framework of miasma, and in this framework the hand-washing results looked like a coincidence. We today look through the framework of germ theory, and this makes Semmelweis look obviously right. The risk is that we are in the same position as the doctors of 1847 with regard to some of our own beliefs, but we cannot see which ones. This suggests a kind of humility is appropriate, although it should not become a belief that nothing is known.

In history the situation is different, because the past does not change but our understanding of it does. For example, the way that the British Empire is taught has changed. In the early twentieth century school textbooks in Britain often presented the empire as a civilizing mission, and now many historians emphasise the violence of colonial rule, such as the Bengal famine of 1943 or the camps in Kenya. Here the passage of time changed what counts as historical knowledge, partly because new sources became available, such as documents released in the archives, and partly because the people asking the questions changed. This is different from the natural sciences, because the second reason is not about evidence but about values and perspectives. Historians today may ask questions that earlier ones did not think of. A defender of the older view might say that we are just replacing one bias with another. I think there is some truth in that, but the more recent accounts use more sources and include the voices of people who were colonised, which earlier accounts largely ignored, so I would say the knowledge has improved and not simply changed.

On the other hand, some claims in history do not change. The date of the Battle of Hastings, 1066, or the fact that the Holocaust happened are not likely to be revised. This suggests that there is a core of well-established facts and a layer of interpretation around it, and that time changes mostly the interpretation. Similarly in science, the boiling point of water at sea level or the fact that the Earth orbits the Sun are not going to be overturned, even if our explanations of them are deepened. So the extent to which time changes knowledge depends on the type of knowledge claim.

It is also worth asking how the passage of time affects the way we gain knowledge, and not only the claims. In the seventeenth century, a claim about the heavens was tested by looking through a telescope, and Galileo's observations of the moons of Jupiter were disputed partly because some people doubted that the instrument showed anything real. Today, claims in particle physics depend on detectors and software that no single person can fully check, so the justification has become more dependent on trusting other people. This suggests that what counts as good evidence is itself something that changes with time, and so the standards for knowledge are not fixed either. I think this is a further reason to say that time changes knowledge, though it also shows that the methods have generally become more careful, with peer review and replication.

I would also like to consider an objection that the question is wrongly put. Someone could say that knowledge is by definition true, and that things which are later shown to be false were never knowledge but only belief. According to this view, the passage of time does not change what counts as knowledge but only reveals what was knowledge all along. This is a possible position, but it has a problem: it means that we can never be sure that we have any knowledge at present, because we cannot know which of our beliefs will be overturned. In practice we have to use the working definition, justified belief accepted by the community, and under this definition time does change what counts.

I should admit that my examples come from Western history and science, and that other traditions treat time and knowledge differently. In some oral traditions knowledge is valued because it has stayed the same across generations, and the fact that it has lasted is part of why it counts as knowledge. For these communities the passage of time can strengthen the status of a claim rather than weaken it. This is a perspective that I have not been able to explore fully, but it suggests that the answer to the question depends on what a community values in knowledge: novelty and correction or continuity and preservation.

In conclusion, the passage of time changes what counts as knowledge to a large extent, but in different ways in different areas. In the natural sciences it narrows and refines claims, as when Newton was shown to be an approximation, and sometimes it replaces them, as with miasma. In history it shifts interpretations, while a core of facts stays stable. In both cases the change is caused partly by new evidence and partly by shifts in what a community is prepared to accept. The lesson for a knower is to hold beliefs with the confidence they deserve at the time, while being ready to revise them.

task: Is the knowledge we gain from experts more reliable than the knowledge we gain for ourselves?
text:
In the modern world we rely on experts for lots of things. When we are ill we go to a doctor, when our car breaks down we go to a mechanic, and when we want to know about the universe we ask a scientist. But do experts really give us more reliable knowledge than the knowledge we get by ourselves? In this essay I will look at this question using the natural sciences and the human sciences and I will argue that in most cases expert knowledge is more reliable, but that there are some exceptions.

First of all, we need to understand what an expert is. An expert is someone who has a lot of knowledge and experience in a particular field. For example a doctor has studied for many years at university and has treated thousands of patients. Reliable knowledge means knowledge that we can trust to be true most of the time. There are different ways of gaining knowledge. We can gain knowledge ourselves through our senses, through reason, through experience or through experiments. We can also gain knowledge from other people, which is called testimony.

In the natural sciences expert knowledge is very important. Imagine that a person has a headache for a week and they search on the internet and decide that they have a brain tumour. This person has gained knowledge for themselves but it is likely to be wrong, because they do not have the training to interpret the symptoms. A doctor, on the other hand, would know that most headaches are caused by stress or dehydration, and would do tests if needed. So in this case the expert knowledge is more reliable. Experts in science also use the scientific method, which means they make hypotheses, do experiments and check the results with other scientists. This is called peer review and it makes the knowledge more reliable because many people check it. A person who just does an experiment by themselves at home does not have this advantage.

Another example is the climate. Nearly all climate scientists agree that global warming is caused by humans. If I look out of my window in a cold winter I might think that the Earth is not getting warmer, but that would be a mistake because I am only looking at one place on one day. The scientists have data from the whole world over many years. So we should trust the experts in this case. This shows that expert knowledge is more reliable than the knowledge we gain for ourselves through our senses, which can be limited.

However, experts are not always right. Experts can make mistakes and sometimes they are biased. For example, in the past some doctors recommended smoking, and some scientists were paid by companies to say that it was safe. Experts can also disagree with each other. If two economists say different things about whether taxes should go up, which one should we believe? This is a problem for the idea that expert knowledge is reliable. We could also say that experts may be too sure of themselves, which is called overconfidence. So we should not trust experts blindly.

In the human sciences, such as psychology and economics, it is even more difficult because human beings are complicated. Economists are often wrong about what will happen to the economy, for example many of them did not predict the financial crisis. Here it might be better to use our own judgement. For instance, a person who has been running a small shop for twenty years may know more about what customers want than an economist who has never worked in a shop. This is a kind of knowledge that comes from experience and it is also valuable. So in this area, the knowledge that we gain for ourselves can be as reliable as expert knowledge, or even more.

Another area to consider is history. Historians are experts on the past, and we usually trust a history textbook more than our own ideas about what happened. For example if I want to know about the causes of the First World War I would read a book by a historian, because they have studied many sources, and I have only seen a few things on television. But historians can also be biased, and they sometimes write from the point of view of their own country. A British book and a German book on the war might say different things. This makes it difficult to say that the expert is always more reliable. We would need to look at many experts, and this takes time.

Art is also an area where the idea of the expert is not clear. A critic might say that a painting is great, but I might not like it. Who is right? Some people think the critic is right because they know more about art, but others think that everyone has their own opinion about what is beautiful. This is a case where the knowledge we gain for ourselves might be just as important as the knowledge from experts.

There are also different perspectives on this question. Some people believe that we should always trust experts because they have more education. Other people think that we should think for ourselves and not just follow what we are told. In some cultures, for example, the knowledge of elders is highly valued, and elders are a kind of expert even if they have no university degrees. Indigenous peoples have knowledge about plants and the environment that has been passed down for many generations, and sometimes scientists have learned from them. This shows that there are different kinds of experts and that expert knowledge is not only from universities.

Another thing to think about is the role of technology. Nowadays we can search for information on Google and we can find answers to nearly everything in a few seconds. This means that people can be more independent than before. Some people say that this makes experts less important. But the problem is that there is a lot of false information on the internet, so it can be hard to know what is true. This means that we still need experts to help us. At the same time, experts also use the internet and computers to do their research, so the line between expert knowledge and our own knowledge is not always clear.

Experts also have to deal with new problems. During the covid pandemic many experts gave advice, and sometimes the advice changed, for example about whether people should wear masks. Some people lost trust in experts because of this. But I think that changing advice is a sign of science working, because scientists change their opinions when there is new evidence. It is a problem when the public does not understand this. This is why communication is important, because experts must explain things clearly, and people must be ready to listen.

Some people say that we should trust the majority opinion of experts. If ninety-seven percent of scientists agree on something then it is probably true. I agree with this to some extent, but history shows that the majority has sometimes been wrong, for example people once believed that the Earth was the centre of the universe. Even so, it is more sensible to trust the majority of experts than to trust one person on the internet.

Furthermore, there is the question of how we can know if someone is an expert. We usually look at their qualifications, their experience and their reputation. But there are fake experts, for example people who say they are doctors on social media but have no real training. This makes it harder to judge. We could also consider whether the expert is working in the area they actually studied. A physicist may be an expert in physics but not an expert in politics, so we should be careful when someone is called an expert in a field that is not their own.

There is also the question of what we mean by reliable. Reliable could mean that the knowledge is true, or that it works in practice, or that it is consistent. A mechanic's knowledge may not be very theoretical but it works, because the car starts after he repairs it. So in this case it is reliable in a practical way. A scientist's knowledge may be more theoretical but still reliable. These are different types of reliability and so it is hard to compare them.

In my opinion, expert knowledge is generally more reliable than the knowledge that we gain for ourselves, because experts have more training, more data and their work is checked by others. However, experts can be wrong, biased and disagree with each other, so we should think critically about what they say. We should also remember that personal experience can sometimes be more reliable, especially in areas where it is about our own lives, such as how we feel or what we like. For example, only I know whether I am happy.

In conclusion, there is no simple answer to the question. It depends on the area of knowledge and on the situation. In the natural sciences experts are usually more reliable, in the human sciences it is less clear, and in everyday life we need both. The best approach is to combine expert knowledge with our own thinking. This will give us the most reliable knowledge. To sum up, experts are generally more reliable but not always, and we need to be critical.

task: Can we trust our emotions as a source of knowledge?
text:
Emotions are a very important part of life and everyone has them. We feel happy, sad, angry and scared. In this essay I am going to talk about whether we can trust our emotions as a source of knowledge. I think that we can trust them sometimes but not always.

Firstly, I will explain what emotions are. Emotions are feelings that we have in our body and mind when something happens. For example when I got my exam results last year I felt very nervous before I opened them and then I felt really happy because I did well. Emotions can be strong and they can change quickly. Some scientists say emotions are chemicals in the brain.

One reason we can trust our emotions is that they tell us things. For example if you feel scared in a dark street then maybe it is dangerous and you should go away. My mum always says that you should trust your gut feeling. When I was younger I was in a shop and I felt that something was wrong with a man who was following me, and I told my dad, and we left the shop. I think this shows that emotions can be a way of knowing because my feeling was right. Also, when we feel love for our family, we know that they are important to us. So emotions give us knowledge about ourselves and the world.

Another reason is that many famous people say that you should follow your heart. Artists use their emotions to make art and music. For example Van Gogh painted his paintings with lots of emotion and people feel something when they see them. So emotions can be knowledge in the arts. This shows that emotions are very useful.

However, there are some reasons why we cannot trust emotions. Sometimes our emotions are wrong. For example when I was angry with my friend I said some things which I did not mean and then I was sorry. If I had trusted my emotion I would have believed my friend was a bad person, but it was not true. Also, people can be happy or sad for no reason, for example because they did not sleep well. This means that emotions are not reliable. In a court of law the judge should not use emotions but only facts. If the judge used emotions then it would not be fair, so we cannot trust emotions here.

In science, scientists are not supposed to use emotions. They use evidence and experiments. If a scientist felt that a medicine worked but the experiment showed that it did not, then the scientist should believe the experiment. So in science emotions are not a good source of knowledge. Reason is better than emotion in this case.

There are also different cultures and they might think about emotions in different ways. In some cultures people show their emotions more and in other cultures they hide their emotions. I think it depends on the person and the culture.

Another time I felt something strongly was when I was choosing my subjects for the IB. I felt really excited about biology and I also felt that I should do economics because my uncle said it was good. I chose biology because I felt happy when I thought about it. Now I am doing biology and I like it, so my emotions were a good source of knowledge here. But my friend chose a subject because she felt that she liked the teacher and then she found out she did not like the subject, so her emotions gave her wrong knowledge. This shows that emotions work sometimes.

I also think that emotions are different for everyone. Some people are more emotional than others and some people hardly ever cry. People who are very emotional might not be good at making decisions. For example my cousin gets upset very easily and then she makes quick choices. I think it is better to wait until you are calm. Doctors have to be calm in an emergency so that they can think properly, but they also have to care about the patient.

In conclusion I think that emotions can be a source of knowledge sometimes, for example in the arts and in dangerous situations, but we cannot always trust them because they can be wrong. We should use both emotion and reason together. This is the best way to get knowledge. Emotions are a very important part of being human and so we should listen to them but we should also think carefully. In my opinion, the answer to the question is that we can trust emotions a little but not completely.

task: Extended Essay in Economics (abridged to about 2000 words, marked as if the full 4000 words continued at this level). Research question: To what extent has the 2018 UK Soft Drinks Industry Levy reduced sugar consumption from soft drinks, and was the change driven by price or by reformulation?
text:
Title: The Sugar Tax Without the Tax Revenue? Evaluating the 2018 UK Soft Drinks Industry Levy

Research question: To what extent has the Soft Drinks Industry Levy (SDIL), introduced in the United Kingdom in April 2018, reduced sugar consumption from soft drinks, and was the reduction driven by consumer price responses or by producer reformulation?

Introduction

Obesity is a market failure in the sense that the private cost of sugary drinks does not reflect the costs to the health service, which are paid by taxpayers. This negative externality, together with imperfect information, provides the standard economic justification for taxing sugar-sweetened beverages. The UK government announced a levy in March 2016, with two tiers: 18 pence per litre for drinks containing 5 to 8 grams of sugar per 100 millilitres, and 24 pence per litre for drinks above 8 grams. Milk-based drinks, pure fruit juices and small producers were exempt. Textbook analysis predicts that a per unit tax will raise price, reduce quantity, and raise revenue, and that the effect on quantity depends on the price elasticity of demand (PED). My interest in this question arose because the levy appears to contradict this prediction. Reports suggested that sugar fell sharply while the revenue was lower than the Treasury had forecast, which implies that firms avoided the tax rather than paying it. This makes the case interesting because it tests whether the standard demand-side model is the right lens.

This essay argues that the levy reduced sugar from soft drinks mainly through producer reformulation, a supply-side response to the tier structure, and that the consumer price response was a secondary mechanism. It uses microeconomic theory, specifically tax incidence, elasticity and the economics of externalities, and evaluates it against published data.

Methodology

I used a secondary-data approach, since a primary survey of consumption by a student could not be representative. The main sources were the Public Health England report on sugar reduction progress between 2015 and 2018 (PHE, 2019), the peer-reviewed study by Scarborough et al. (2020) on the content and price of drinks before and after the announcement, and the Office for Budget Responsibility forecasts for the levy revenue. I chose these because they use sales-weighted data, which matters because an unweighted average of sugar content would treat a niche drink the same as a bestselling one. For the demand-side analysis I used an elasticity estimate from Andreyeva, Long and Brownell (2010), a review of US studies that puts own-price elasticity of soft drinks at around -0.8, and I tested the sensitivity of my calculations to values between -0.5 and -1.2. A limitation is that US estimates may not apply to the UK. A further limitation is that the data is aggregate, so I cannot separate effects on different income groups. I rejected a difference-in-differences comparison with another country because no clean comparator exists, since many countries were changing sugar policy at the same time.

Part 1: The theoretical prediction

In a standard diagram for a per unit tax, the supply curve shifts upward by the amount of the tax. If we take a 330 millilitre can of a high-sugar drink priced at about 70 pence, the 24 pence per litre levy equals approximately 7.9 pence per can, if it is fully passed on to consumers, which would be an 11 percent rise in price. With a PED of -0.8, quantity demanded would fall by about 9 percent. If PED were -0.5 the fall would be 5.6 percent, and at -1.2 it would be 13 percent. Sugar consumption from taxed drinks would therefore fall by roughly 6 to 13 percent through price alone, if the price rise was entirely passed on. The incidence of the tax depends on the relative elasticities: if supply is more elastic than demand, consumers bear most of the burden. This is the benchmark against which I measure the actual result. If the actual sugar reduction is far larger than 13 percent, there must be another mechanism.

Part 2: What happened to sugar content

PHE (2019) reported that the sales-weighted average sugar content of drinks in scope of the levy fell by 28.8 percent between 2015 and 2018, a much bigger fall than the demand-side calculation would predict. Moreover, much of this fall occurred between the announcement in 2016 and the implementation in 2018, which means that firms responded to the announcement and not to the actual price change. Scarborough et al. (2020) found that the proportion of drinks above the 8 gram threshold decreased substantially, and that many drinks moved under 5 grams, where no levy applied. Examples include Irn-Bru and Ribena, which cut sugar and replaced it with sweeteners, while Coca-Cola Classic was not reformulated but was promoted with a zero-sugar version.

The economic logic is clear. The tiered structure is a threshold tax, and it creates a discontinuity in the cost function. A producer facing a tax of 24 pence per litre on a drink with 8.1 grams of sugar, which could be moved to 4.9 grams at a small cost of reformulation, has a strong incentive to reformulate, particularly where the cost of artificial sweeteners is lower than the tax. In effect the producer's marginal cost of avoiding the tax is lower than the cost of paying it. This is why the levy was more effective in changing the product than in changing consumer behaviour, and why the revenue was lower than forecast. The levy was designed with a clear target: it taxed the sugar content and not the volume, which makes avoidance by reformulation profitable.

Part 3: The consumer response

Scarborough et al. (2020) report that the prices of drinks in the highest tier rose only slightly, and that firms did not pass on the whole levy; many shifted the cost across their range, increasing the price of some lower-tier drinks or reducing the price of exempt drinks. This is a form of cross-subsidy that weakens the price signal. If the price rise for high-sugar drinks was far below 11 percent, the demand-side effect on those drinks was small, probably below the 6 to 13 percent estimated above. Pack sizes were also changed, for example some cans were made smaller. A further consideration is that the elasticity for a specific brand is greater than for the category, since consumers can switch to competing brands, but in the case of this levy most brands were all affected in the same way.

It would be wrong, however, to say the consumer response was nil. The volume of levied drinks sold fell slightly, while sales of zero-sugar drinks grew. Even so, the PHE data suggests that sales volumes of soft drinks overall continued to rise, so the sugar reduction is attributable to the lower sugar per litre, not to the lower litres consumed. I estimate, by decomposing the change in total sugar sold into volume and concentration effects, that the concentration effect accounts for the large majority of the reduction. The decomposition is approximate because it combines figures from two sources with different product definitions.

Part 4: Evaluation of effectiveness and alternative explanations

The conclusion that reformulation dominated depends on the assumption that firms responded to the levy. An alternative explanation is that there was a pre-existing trend towards lower sugar, caused by the Public Health England sugar reduction programme and by changing consumer tastes. This is a serious objection, since the voluntary programme started in 2016 too. However, the voluntary programme had set a target of 20 percent reduction by 2020 across many food categories, and soft drinks were the only category that exceeded it by a wide margin, which suggests that the levy, with its financial incentive, was the key difference. Even so, I cannot fully separate the two effects with the available data, and this limits the confidence of my conclusion.

A second question is whether reducing sugar per litre is the same as reducing consumption of sugar. If consumers who drink diet versions replace sugar elsewhere in their diet, the benefit is lower. Evidence on this is weak, but the Family Food survey shows no obvious increase in confectionery purchases. A third issue is equity. Sugary drinks are consumed more by lower-income households, so the tax would be regressive if the price rose substantially, but since the main response was reformulation, low-income households received the health benefit without paying much of the tax. This is a positive for the policy. On the other hand, the design may be less effective for other externalities, because the reformulated drinks contain sweeteners with uncertain long-term effects.

Conclusion

The levy did reduce sugar from soft drinks, by a substantial amount by the measure of sales-weighted sugar concentration, and the evidence points to producer reformulation as the dominant mechanism, rather than the consumer price response, which at best would explain a minority of the fall. This supports a revision of the textbook model: where a tax is structured with thresholds, the supply response to the incentive can be larger than the demand response to the price. As a result, a levy can succeed on health grounds while raising little revenue, which means that these two aims are in conflict and policymakers should decide which one they prefer. The conclusion is limited by the lack of a counterfactual and by the use of aggregate data. A fuller study could use household purchase data from Kantar to examine the response by income group.

Bibliography

Andreyeva, T., Long, M. and Brownell, K. (2010) The impact of food prices on consumption: a systematic review of research on the price elasticity of demand for food. American Journal of Public Health, 100(2), pp. 216-222.
Public Health England (2019) Sugar reduction: report on progress between 2015 and 2018. London: PHE.
Scarborough, P. et al. (2020) Impact of the announcement and implementation of the UK Soft Drinks Industry Levy on sugar content, price, product size and number of available soft drinks in the UK, 2015-19. PLOS Medicine, 17(2).
Office for Budget Responsibility (2018) Economic and fiscal outlook. London: OBR.

Reflections on planning and progress

My first plan was to survey students at my school about their drink choices before and after the levy, but my supervisor, Dr Mansour, pointed out that students would not remember and the sample would not be representative. This was a turning point: I switched to secondary data, and I narrowed my question from whether the levy worked to why it worked. My first draft was too descriptive and simply listed the findings of the reports. After a meeting in which Dr Mansour asked me what the theory predicted, I added the benchmark calculation in Part 1, which made the analysis stronger. I found it difficult to combine data from sources with different definitions of soft drinks, and I had to spend a week working out which figures could be compared. If I did this again I would start by contacting the authors for the underlying data. I learned that an economic model is a starting point for judging the evidence and not a conclusion, and I became more careful in distinguishing correlation from causation.
