text:
Title: The Corruption of the American Dream in The Great Gatsby

Research question: How does F. Scott Fitzgerald present the American Dream in The Great Gatsby?

Introduction

The Great Gatsby, published in 1925, is often called the great American novel. It is set in the summer of 1922 on Long Island and in New York City, and it is narrated by Nick Carraway, a young man from the Midwest who works in the bond business. The central character is Jay Gatsby, a mysterious millionaire who throws lavish parties in the hope of winning back Daisy Buchanan, the woman he loved before the war. The American Dream is the belief that anyone, through hard work and determination, can achieve success and prosperity, regardless of the circumstances of their birth. In this essay I will examine how Fitzgerald presents this dream in the novel. I will argue that Fitzgerald presents the American Dream as corrupted by materialism, and that he shows it to be an illusion that cannot be achieved by people like Gatsby. I will look at the characters of Gatsby and Daisy, the symbols of the green light and the Valley of Ashes, and the ending of the novel.

Methodology

For this essay I used the novel as my primary source. I read it twice, and made notes on quotations connected to wealth, dreams and class. I then used some secondary sources: a critical introduction to the novel by Matthew Bruccoli, a biography of Fitzgerald and a study guide, as well as some articles I found online. I chose these to give me different views on the book. I also looked at some information about the 1920s in America, such as Prohibition and the stock market boom. My approach is a close reading of the text, looking at language, imagery and symbolism, and relating it to the historical context.

The dream and Gatsby

Gatsby is the character who most clearly represents the American Dream. He was born James Gatz to poor farming parents in North Dakota, and he reinvented himself as Jay Gatsby after meeting the millionaire Dan Cody. In Chapter 6 Nick tells us that Gatsby "sprang from his Platonic conception of himself". This phrase shows that Gatsby created his own identity, which fits the idea that in America you can be anything. However, Fitzgerald also shows that Gatsby's wealth comes from criminal activity such as bootlegging with Meyer Wolfsheim. This suggests that the way to the dream in the 1920s is through corruption instead of hard work. The dream is therefore shown as having lost its moral basis.

Gatsby's mansion and his parties are also a symbol of his dream. Nick describes the parties in Chapter 3, with "men and girls came and went like moths among the whisperings and the champagne and the stars". The simile of moths suggests that the guests are attracted to the light but are shallow and temporary, and moths may also be burnt by the light. Fitzgerald uses the long list of food and drink and the music to show a world of excess. But nobody at the party really knows Gatsby, and at his funeral almost nobody comes. This shows that the wealth did not bring him real happiness or real relationships.

Daisy and the dream

Daisy is the object of Gatsby's dream. She is described as having a voice "full of money", which Gatsby says in Chapter 7. This shows that for Gatsby, Daisy is not only a person but also a symbol of wealth and social status. She belongs to old money, and Gatsby, who is new money, cannot truly be part of that world. Tom Buchanan, her husband, is from a rich family and he is arrogant and unfaithful, which shows that old money does not mean moral values. When Daisy chooses Tom over Gatsby in the hotel scene, it shows that the class barrier is stronger than the dream. Daisy also lets Gatsby take the blame for the death of Myrtle Wilson, and she and Tom retreat into "their money or their vast carelessness". This line shows that rich people can escape the consequences, while Gatsby pays with his life.

Symbols: the green light and the Valley of Ashes

The green light at the end of Daisy's dock is the most famous symbol in the novel. In Chapter 1 Gatsby is seen stretching out his arms toward it. The colour green can suggest hope, money and envy. It is far away across the bay, so it also suggests that the dream is out of reach. At the end of the novel Nick says that Gatsby "believed in the green light, the orgastic future that year by year recedes before us". The word recedes shows that the future always moves away, so that the dream can never be achieved. This is one of the main points of the book.

The Valley of Ashes is the opposite of the green light. It is a grey industrial area between West Egg and New York, where the poor live, for example George Wilson, who owns a garage. It is described as a "fantastic farm where ashes grow like wheat". Fitzgerald uses this image to show that the wealth of the rich is built on the poverty of the poor. Over the valley are the eyes of Doctor T. J. Eckleburg on a billboard, which some critics say represent God watching over a moral wasteland. The Valley of Ashes shows that the American Dream is not available to everyone, since people like Wilson work hard and do not succeed. This challenges the idea that hard work leads to success.

Nick Carraway as narrator

Another important part of how Fitzgerald presents the dream is through Nick. Nick is the narrator, so we see everything through his eyes. He says at the start that he is "inclined to reserve all judgements", but throughout the novel he does judge people. He is both inside and outside the story, because he lives next to Gatsby but he is not rich himself. This allows him to describe the rich people and also to criticise them. At the end he decides to go back to the Midwest because he is disgusted by the East, which suggests that the moral values of the Midwest are better than those of New York. The narrator is therefore a way for Fitzgerald to show his own opinion about the dream. Some critics say that Nick is unreliable because he is clearly fascinated by Gatsby, and I think that this is true, since he says that Gatsby had "an extraordinary gift for hope" and "a romantic readiness". The reader needs to decide how far to trust Nick.

Context

Fitzgerald wrote the novel in the Jazz Age, a period of great economic growth and cultural change after the First World War. Prohibition made alcohol illegal and created opportunities for gangsters, such as the character of Wolfsheim who is based on Arnold Rothstein. The stock market was booming and many people were getting rich quickly, before the crash of 1929. Fitzgerald himself was from the Midwest and he lived a life of parties and spending with his wife Zelda, so he knew about the glamour and the emptiness. This context helps us understand that Fitzgerald was critical of the culture of materialism that he saw around him.

Different readings

Some critics read the novel as a tragedy of a romantic hero. In this view, Gatsby is admirable because of his hope, and Nick says "they're a rotten crowd. You're worth the whole damn bunch put together". Other critics say that Gatsby is not a hero but a criminal who wants to buy love. I think that both readings are possible and that Fitzgerald intended Gatsby to be a mixture of both. This ambiguity makes the book more interesting. Also, the novel can be read as a criticism of America, but Nick also says at the end that Gatsby's dream was "already behind him", suggesting a nostalgia for an older and purer idea of America.

Conclusion

To conclude, Fitzgerald presents the American Dream as corrupted and impossible. Through Gatsby he shows that the dream is based on wealth and that it ends in disappointment. Through Daisy and Tom he shows that class barriers cannot be crossed, and through the green light and the Valley of Ashes he uses symbolism to show the distance between dream and reality. The final image of boats "borne back ceaselessly into the past" suggests that people can never escape their origins. Fitzgerald therefore criticises the American Dream, but he also seems to admire the hope that it represents. This makes The Great Gatsby a complex and powerful book that is still relevant today.

Bibliography

Fitzgerald, F. S. (1925) The Great Gatsby. New York: Scribner.
Bruccoli, M. (1993) Introduction to The Great Gatsby. Cambridge University Press.
Study guide on The Great Gatsby, SparkNotes website.
Various websites on the 1920s and Prohibition.

Reflections on planning and progress

At the start I found it hard to choose a research question and my supervisor, Ms Hughes, helped me to make it clearer. I read the book twice and made notes. My first draft was too long and I had to cut some parts. I found it difficult to find good critical sources, so I used some websites. I think I improved my essay writing and my time management, and I learned how to use quotations. If I did it again I would start earlier and use more secondary sources. I am happy with my essay.

Title: The Atomic Bombs on Japan

Research question: Was the dropping of the atomic bombs on Japan justified?

Introduction

In August 1945 the United States dropped two atomic bombs on Japan, one on Hiroshima on 6 August and another on Nagasaki on 9 August. These were the first and only times nuclear weapons have been used in war. About 140,000 people died in Hiroshima and about 70,000 in Nagasaki, many of them civilians. Japan surrendered on 15 August and the Second World War ended. This is one of the most controversial events in history and people still argue about it. In this essay I will look at the reasons why the bombs were dropped and I will decide if it was justified. I will use books and websites to find the information.

Background

The Second World War began in 1939 when Germany invaded Poland. The United States entered the war in 1941 after Japan attacked Pearl Harbor. By 1945 Germany had been defeated but Japan still fought on. The US had been fighting its way across the Pacific, island by island, and the battles at Iwo Jima and Okinawa were very bloody. The Americans lost many soldiers and the Japanese fought to the death and used kamikaze pilots. President Roosevelt died in April 1945 and Harry Truman became president. Truman did not know about the Manhattan Project until after he became president. The Manhattan Project was the secret programme to build an atomic bomb, which was led by J. Robert Oppenheimer and tested in New Mexico on 16 July 1945.

Reasons for the bombing

The main reason that the bombs were dropped was to end the war quickly. The Americans were planning an invasion of Japan called Operation Downfall, and the generals said that it would cost about a million American lives. Truman wanted to avoid this. The bomb would force Japan to surrender without an invasion. This saved lives on both sides, because the Japanese would also have lost many more people in an invasion. So the bombs saved more lives than they took.

Another reason was to show the Soviet Union how powerful the US was. The Cold War was beginning and Stalin was becoming a rival. Some historians say that this was the real reason. Also, the US had spent two billion dollars on the Manhattan Project and so they wanted to use it. Another reason is revenge for Pearl Harbor, because many Americans hated the Japanese.

Arguments that it was justified

Many people say that it was justified. First, Japan refused to surrender when the Allies issued the Potsdam Declaration on 26 July. The Japanese prime minister said that they would ignore it. Second, the Japanese military was very strong and many leaders wanted to fight to the end. Third, the bomb ended the war quickly and so it saved lives. Fourth, in war many civilians had been killed anyway, for example in the firebombing of Tokyo in March 1945, which killed more than 100,000 people. So the atomic bomb was not much different from other bombing.

Arguments that it was not justified

Other people say that it was not justified. First, the bombs killed many innocent civilians, including women and children, and this is a war crime. Second, Japan was already nearly defeated, because the navy had been destroyed and there was a blockade, and so it was going to surrender soon anyway. Third, the US could have done a demonstration of the bomb on an uninhabited island so that Japan could see how powerful it was. Fourth, the bombs caused radiation sickness and cancer for many years, and this was cruel. Some American military leaders, such as Eisenhower, later said that the bomb was not necessary. The Soviet Union also declared war on Japan on 8 August, and some historians think that this was the real reason Japan surrendered.

The effects of the bombs

The effects of the bombs were terrible. In Hiroshima the bomb, which was called Little Boy, exploded about 600 metres above the city and destroyed about 70 percent of the buildings. The temperature was very high and people were burnt in an instant. In Nagasaki the bomb was called Fat Man and it was a plutonium bomb. The city was in hills and so the damage was a bit less than in Hiroshima. Many survivors, who are called hibakusha, suffered from radiation sickness and some people discriminated against them afterwards. These effects show how awful nuclear weapons are.

The role of the Emperor

One more thing to say is that the Japanese Emperor Hirohito made a radio broadcast on 15 August in which he announced the surrender. He said that the enemy had begun to employ a new and most cruel bomb. This shows that the bombs were important in the decision. Some of the Japanese leaders wanted to continue and there was nearly a coup to stop the surrender. So we can see that the bombs were needed to make the Emperor decide.

My opinion

I think that the bombs were justified because they ended the war and saved lives. Although it was terrible that so many people died, an invasion would have been much worse. I read in a book that the invasion would have cost a million lives. Truman made the right decision. However, I also feel that it was very sad and that nuclear weapons should never be used again.

Conclusion

In conclusion, the atomic bombs were dropped on Hiroshima and Nagasaki to end the war. There are arguments for and against. The people who think it was justified say that it saved lives, and the people who think it was not justified say that it killed civilians. In my opinion it was justified because the war ended quickly. This is still a controversial topic today.

Bibliography

Wikipedia: Atomic bombings of Hiroshima and Nagasaki.
History.com website.
BBC Bitesize, World War Two.
A history textbook from my school library.

Reflections on planning and progress

I chose this topic because I am interested in World War Two. I looked for information on the internet and in the library. It was difficult to find good books. I wrote the essay in about two weeks. My supervisor read it and said it was fine. I learned a lot about the atomic bombs and I enjoyed writing the essay.
